messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 27
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: African
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Taxi/Uber Driver
- Trauma Type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
- Pcl5: 56

He sits on the edge of the armchair, a large man folded into himself, his knees bouncing slightly. His jacket stays on. His baseball cap stays low. It is the fourth session, and he still scans the room the way he scans his rearview mirror—constant, automatic, searching for threat. When I ask him what brought him here, he doesn't start with the present. He starts with the car.

He was seven when his uncle took them in. His father was absent, his mother worked double shifts, and his uncle became the authority in the house. The discipline was regular, ritualistic. He remembers the belt most clearly. The way his uncle would fold it, double it over, tap it against his own palm. But worse than the belt was the car ride that preceded it.

“He would make me get in the backseat,” he says, his voice flat. “No talking. He would drive for twenty, thirty minutes. Out of the city. Into the fields. I would watch the back of his neck. The way his jaw moved. I knew what was coming. The waiting was the worst part.”

He would pull over into a clearing. He would tell him to put his hands on the headrest in front, to brace himself. He smelled like sweat and machine oil. There was a rag he used to gag him so the neighbors wouldn't hear. The taste of that rag, he says, never left his mouth. The beatings continued until he was fourteen, when he grew tall enough to fight back. He left home that year. He hasn't spoken to his uncle since.

He is twenty-seven now. He drives for Uber. He works the night shift mostly.

He describes his job as a constant negotiation with his nervous system. Every passenger who gets into his backseat is a potential reenactment. He watches them in the mirror—their hands, their posture, the tone of their voice. He has memorized the lock button. His thumb rests on it. When a passenger leans forward to give directions, he flinches. When they touch the headrest, he freezes. Last month, a drunk passenger tapped him on the shoulder from the backseat, and he slammed on the brakes in the middle of an intersection. He almost hit the man. He pulled over, shaking, and told him to get out. The passenger complained, and he received a warning from the platform.

He has strict rules now. No rides longer than fifteen minutes. No passengers who look intoxicated. He keeps the music loud enough to fill the silence, because silence takes him back. The quiet car, the waiting, the inevitability. If there is too much quiet, he hears his own breathing, and he is in the field again.

He lives alone. The apartment is sparse, functional. He sleeps in his clothes. He has tried dating, but the last woman touched his back in bed, and he threw her off him instinctively. He felt shame for days. He has not tried since.

He believes the world is divided into drivers and passengers. Those who have power and those who do not. He has spent his entire adult life making sure he is never in the backseat again. But the irony is not lost on him: his freedom is a car with strangers in the back, his thumb hovering over the lock button, his heart racing at every sudden movement.

He came to therapy because he is tired of being afraid. Not of his uncle—that fear is old, worn smooth. He is afraid of himself. Of what he might do when the trigger gets pulled too hard. He looks at his hands, which are large and still, and he says quietly: “These hands used to be small. I couldn't fight back. Now they're big. And I don't trust them when I'm scared.”
